name: International Refugee Assistance Project: legal services (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: where IRAP's clients wait for a pathway (a judgment, as IRAP publishes no split): Central American families seeking reunification 40% (the model's wh_client_share), and its Jordan and Lebanon offices' refugees, US-affiliated Afghans in Afghanistan and Pakistan, refugees in Kenya referred by partners, and asylum seekers and status cases in the US, the other 60%.
summary: The International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP), a US legal aid organisation, represented or counselled 4,884 refugees and other displaced people in the year to August 2025 from offices in New York, Washington, Berlin, Amman and Beirut, helping them reach safety through resettlement, family reunification and humanitarian or Special Immigrant Visas. This model values a client brought to safety by the rise in their consumption from what refugees live on while they wait to what resettled refugees consume in a rich country, for the decades the move lasts, plus the deaths averted while they would otherwise have waited in danger. With a tenth of a year's clients judged to reach safety in a year (IRAP publishes no count), 40% of those moves not otherwise happening and the rest brought about a year and a half sooner and about three quarters of the credit IRAP's, it comes to about 0.07 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, below the site's global-health median: the casework costs about $4,700 a client and few clients get out in a year, fewer still after the US suspended refugee admissions in January 2025. The biggest uncertainty is the share of clients the casework brings to safety, a judgment, so the model is discounted by the shared missing-data slider; IRAP's litigation and policy work is a separate model.

sections.title: Effect per person
sections.explainer: What a year of IRAP's casework does for each client: the chance it brings them to safety in a safe, richer country, and what that move is worth in consumption and in deaths averted while they would otherwise have waited in danger.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for how far the estimates can be trusted, for moves that would have happened without IRAP, for credit shared with volunteers and the governments that process and receive refugees, and for the wait until the year's casework turns into arrivals.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.explainer: The accounts' Other Programs column: Western Hemisphere migration (legal aid, legal information and advocacy for family reunification from Latin America, including the Bay Area Family Reunification Initiative), the Human Rights Defender pathways programme, legal fellows' stipends and systemic advocacy. Most of it is casework whose clients are in the count below, so it is costed here with Legal Services. Its systemic-advocacy part (a small share) is costed here, while the wins it contributes to are credited in charityevals' model of IRAP's litigation and policy work. Moving a judged share of this column to the advocacy model would split one accounts column between two models' lines (normalization.md 2.17); the cost of the systemic-advocacy part is small (a few percent of this model) and stays here.

source.title: IRAP, Impact Under Fire: 2025 Annual Report (fiscal year September 2024 to August 2025)
source.page: p. 7, Representing and Reuniting Separated Families Around the World
source.quote: This past year, IRAP served 4,884 clients, and of all of our cases, more than 30% included family members seeking reunion with their loved ones.

rows.explainer: IRAP's own count of the people it represented or counselled in the fiscal year (its president's letter, p. 3: 'we served over 4,800 people through legal representation and counseling'), across its US, Jordan, Lebanon and Europe teams and the Western Hemisphere programme. We read it as people, each counted once; family members who travel on a client's case without being counted are not added. The nearly 300,000 people reached with legal information online are not in this count; their benefit is in the unmodelled share below.

rows.label: Cost per client
rows.explainer: Context: about $4,700 a client, against a few hundred dollars a person for most relief.

rows.label: Share of the year's clients who reach lasting safety (arrivals a year over clients a year)
rows.explainer: IRAP publishes no count of clients who reached safety in fiscal year 2025, so this is the yearly flow: people who reach a safe country in a year against the clients served that year (Convention 3), whether or not IRAP made the difference (that is the counterfactual below). Anchors: the 2025 report's explicit counts (55 Syrians from Lebanon, two dozen green cards, 30 French asylum visa applications, 399 people helped toward family reunification in Europe) give at least about 4%; the 2023 report's 961 people helped to rejoin family against 3,497 clients, about 27%, is the high end; in 2022 IRAP reported a positive outcome in 79% of represented cases with a known outcome. Fiscal year 2025 was below the 2023 rate because the US suspended refugee admissions on 20 January 2025. Cases that only secure status for people already safe (green cards) are not moves and are counted in the unmodelled share instead. Our judgment: 10%, from 4% to 27%. The biggest single uncertainty in the model.

rows.label: Death rate of the clients while they wait (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: From the row below.

rows.label: Death rate of IRAP's clients while they wait (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: The shared IRAP figure (facts/irap.json), with its anchors there: refugees in first countries of asylum and people at risk where they are; 0.007, from 0.004 to 0.015.

rows.label: Death rate once safe in a rich country (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for both IRAP models (facts/irap.json): only the excess over it counts.

rows.label: Share of the clients' excess mortality removed
rows.explainer: A client who reaches safety leaves the whole excess behind; one who doesn't keeps it. So the share removed for the clients reached is the share who reach safety.

rows.label: Years a client would otherwise have stayed in danger
rows.explainer: The shared IRAP figure (facts/irap.json): 3 years, from 1 to 5.

rows.label: Deaths averted per client (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the years of danger, discounted at the shared rate, times the share removed.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Most clients are adults; children come on family cases (more than 30% of cases involve reunification), and children are about four in ten of refugees worldwide (UNHCR). Children under five die at higher rates than older children, but most of the excess the clients face (violence, targeted threats) falls on adults: our judgment 0.1, from 0.03 to 0.2, anchored on that family composition rather than a cause-specific WHO split, as the excess has no single cause.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: School-age children are about a quarter of refugee families but die at low rates and are rarely the targets of the threats; a judgment, 0.12, from 0.05 to 0.25, on the same anchor.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The clients are mostly working-age adults, and targeted violence falls on them; the rest at 50 and over.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per client, in DALYs
rows.explainer: Not counted separately: the trauma and anxiety of waiting in danger, and the better health care of a rich country, are in the unmodelled share below rather than guessed as disability weights.

rows.label: Share of clients who are Central American and other Western Hemisphere families
rows.explainer: The Bay Area Family Reunification Initiative alone gave representation or counselling to 3,676 family members between May 2024 and the 2025 report (p. 7), a large part of the 4,884 clients; the rest are refugees served from Amman, Beirut, Europe and the US. Our judgment 40%, from 20% to 60%.

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person a year while they wait (2024 US prices, PPP)
rows.explainer: Clients' consumption a year, a blend of the Western Hemisphere families (Honduras's survey mean, @survey_consumption.hnd_survey_mean_2021ppp_day, standing in for Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador) and the refugees waiting elsewhere (the shared IRAP figure), in 2021 PPP dollars a day, over the year, in 2024 US prices: the same prices as the US survey figure it is compared with, so the ratio is a real one (no market exchange rate enters). A geometric blend would be lower; the arithmetic one is the cautious reading of the ln gain.

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person a year once resettled (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: US household-survey spending per person (Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024) times the share resettled refugees consume (facts/irap.json). The US stands in for every destination; Europe's lower consumption is in that share's range.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per client, discounted
rows.explainer: For a client who reaches safety, consumption rises from what they live on while waiting to what refugees consume once resettled, about sevenfold, for the years the move lasts (facts/irap.json), discounted at the shared rate; times the share who reach safety. About 2.8 log points per client: above the family's usual bound of 3 only in the high case, because a move to a rich country multiplies a poor person's consumption for decades, which no handout does (the place premium: the same worker earns several times more in the US than at home, Clemens, Montenegro and Pritchett 2019).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The consumption gain rests on survey data for the two places and the place-premium literature, which compares the same people in different countries; the main doubts are whether refugees consume as the US poorest fifth do (in the shared share's range) and selection: IRAP's clients may differ from refugees in general. 0.8, from 0.6 to 1, as for our other relief models whose effect is a judgment built on solid comparisons (ShelterBox 0.8).

rows.label: Share of the moves that would never have happened without IRAP's casework
rows.explainer: Many of IRAP's clients would eventually get out without it: UNHCR refers refugees for resettlement, other legal-aid groups (HIAS, RefugePoint, local partners) take some cases, and some families would succeed alone. But IRAP takes the cases with barriers (denials, appeals, documents a family can't get, family reunification rules), where representation matters most: in US immigration courts represented detained immigrants won about ten times as often as unrepresented ones (Eagly and Shafer 2015). A slot one client wins in a capped programme can be one another refugee doesn't get; caps rarely bound in 2023-2025 (US admissions below the ceiling, family reunification uncapped). Our judgment: 40% would never have happened, from 20% to 70%; the rest would have come later (next row).

rows.label: Years sooner the casework brings the moves that would have come anyway
rows.explainer: Where a refugee would have got out without IRAP (another lawyer, a UNHCR referral, a later appeal), the casework mostly brings the move forward: appeals and family reunification cases without counsel stall for years. Our judgment 1.5 years, from 0.5 to 4.

rows.label: Share of the moves' value that wouldn't have come without IRAP (moves that never would have, plus years brought forward)
rows.explainer: The moves that would never have happened count in full; those that would have come anyway count for the years they are brought forward, as the discounted value of those first years over the discounted value of all the years the gain lasts (both at the shared rate).
rows.formula: cf_never_share + (1 - cf_never_share) * min(1, pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_sooner) / pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, @irap.years_gain_lasts))

rows.label: Hours given by IRAP's pro bono lawyers and student volunteers, fiscal year 2025

source.title: IRAP, Impact Under Fire: 2025 Annual Report (fiscal year September 2024 to August 2025)
source.page: p. 10, Our Pro Bono Partners and Student Chapters
source.quote: Indeed, in Fiscal Year 2025, IRAP's network of pro bono partners and student volunteers provided more than 23,657 hours of service valued at $20.5 million.

rows.explainer: Volunteers' unpaid time behind the same casework. IRAP values it at $20.5 million at law-firm rates; the site values volunteer time at the shared hourly value (Convention 2) in the next row.

rows.label: Value of an hour of IRAP's pro bono lawyers' and students' time (US$)
rows.explainer: Convention 2 values volunteers at the local wage for the work they do. Most of the 23,657 hours are attorneys' (the report's 670 private attorneys), the rest law students'. Anchors: a US lawyer's median wage of about $73 an hour (BLS occupational statistics, 2024) and the site's general volunteer hour (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2025, $36) for students. Our judgment $55, from $36 to $90.

rows.label: Volunteers' time, at the shared value of a volunteer hour
rows.explainer: The hours at a lawyer's and student's wage (above). At the law-firm rates IRAP uses ($20.5 million) it would be far larger; the site values volunteers at what they would earn, not what firms bill.

rows.label: Others' resources behind the moves (UNHCR, governments, partner NGOs), as a share of IRAP's cost
rows.explainer: A move to safety also takes UNHCR's referral, the receiving government's processing (interviews, security checks, medical exams) and its reception and placement grants, and partners' local work. These cost a few thousand dollars for each refugee resettled, against IRAP's roughly $50,000 of cost for each client it brings to safety, plus partners' work on shared cases: our judgment 0.3, from 0.1 to 0.8.

rows.label: IRAP's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: IRAP's cost over everyone's: its own, the volunteers' time and the others' resources above (Convention 2).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Nothing more here: the share reaching safety above is already per client counted, whatever service each received.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: IRAP takes no government money (2025 report: 'without a single dollar of government funding') and no government would fund this casework instead; big foundation grants (The Audacious Project's $53 million over 2022-2027) were given anyway. 1, from 0.9 to 1.05.

rows.label: Years from the year's casework to the arrivals it brings
rows.explainer: Visas, referrals and appeals worked on in a year lead to arrivals months to years later (security checks, travel); about a year, from 0.3 to 2.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until arrival
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: IRAP counts its clients but publishes no count of who reached safety because of its work, and no controlled evaluation exists: the share reaching safety is our judgment, so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Extra moves to safety a year from IRAP's online legal information
rows.explainer: IRAP's online legal information reached over 292,138 people in 2025 (report p. 8). Self-help information rarely decides a case on its own; if one reader in 30,000 reaches safety who otherwise wouldn't, that is about 10 moves a year, from none to 100 (one in 3,000).

rows.label: Legal information to about 290,000 people, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The extra moves from the legal information (each a move that otherwise wouldn't happen) as a share of the moves the casework brings that otherwise wouldn't happen (clients × share reaching safety × share that never would have).

rows.label: Other legal benefits (green cards, protected status, avoiding removal), as a share
rows.explainer: Part of the casework secures status for people already safe (green cards, citizenship, protection from deportation), which is not counted as a move to safety above: worth much less a person than a move, but real; 8%, from 0 to 20%. The 80 refugees resettled under the Pacito v. Trump injunctions are counted in charityevals' model of IRAP's litigation, not here.

rows.label: Safety, family reunion and health beyond consumption, as a share
rows.explainer: Consumption misses the relief of being safe and of families reunited (more than 30% of cases) and the long-run health of living in a rich country; 10%, from 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Remittances to family left behind, less early costs to host countries, as a share
rows.explainer: Resettled refugees send money to relatives still waiting (a gain for very poor people); host countries pay reception costs in the first years, mostly repaid in taxes later. Net slightly positive, from -5% to +10%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The sum of the four shares above.

rows.label: Income gained and deaths averted, in GiveWell units of value (before adjustments)
Income gained and deaths averted, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained, in WELLBYs
rows.explainer: Not counted: the model values the move by consumption and deaths, which the wellbeing gain would largely repeat; the part beyond consumption is in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Healthy years counted directly (before adjustments)
Years of healthy life
rows.explainer: Every outcome, each in healthy years by its own unit's conversion, times the adjustments, plus the unmodelled share.
